extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, district court judges, and litigation practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on whether and how district courts should conduct Markman claim-construction proceedings (live hearings, written submissions, or post-trial rulings) and when hearings are advisable. Focuses on procedural options and practical considerations in jury-tried patent infringement cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction is a matter of law for the court
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The construction of a patent, including terms of art within its claim, is exclusively within the province of the court.’ (Markman v. Westview, Justice Souter opinion.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the controlling legal principle: interpretation of patent claims, including disputed technical and non-technical terms, is for judges, not juries, and thus is treated as a question of law. Use this as the baseline for allocating responsibility between judge and jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markman does not require a formal, separate Markman hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Markman does not expressly require the so-called A Markman hearing, a hearing at which nothing but claim interpretation is at issue.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although many practitioners assume a discrete pretrial claim-construction hearing is required, the Supreme Court decision itself does not mandate such a proceeding. Whether to hold a separate Markman hearing depends on local rule, local case law, and judicial preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-trial decision (JMOL) can satisfy Markman obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit has stated a district court may satisfy its obligation by ruling on claim construction in a motion for judgment as a matter of law after a jury verdict (i.e., post-trial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may allow a case to go to a jury without an advance claim construction and later decide construction post-verdict via JMOL. This is an acceptable way to discharge the court’s duty under Markman and is a procedural alternative to holding a pretrial hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local rules and local case law may mandate pretrial Markman hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Some district courts have required pretrial Markman hearings (example: C.D. Cal. held a pretrial hearing is required; N.D. Cal. adopted local rules providing procedures for such hearings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though Markman itself does not mandate hearings, practitioners must check and follow district-specific local rules or controlling local precedents that may impose a requirement for a pretrial claim-construction hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judges may decide claim construction on paper records and written submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Nothing in Markman requires a hearing in the formal sense of a set date, oral argument, and witnesses,’ and the larger trend in courts is toward decisions on paper records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts increasingly rely on written briefs, claim-construction briefs, and documentary records rather than live hearings. Parties should prepare thorough written submissions because judges may resolve construction without live argument or testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances favoring live Markman hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings may be advisable when judges prefer to hear oral argument in their deliberative pace or when 'highly technical testimony' is required to resolve claim meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the judge anticipates benefit from oral advocacy or needs to evaluate complex technical evidence or witness testimony, a live Markman hearing can be useful. Scheduling such hearings to fit judges’ routines and deliberative preferences is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical practical procedure when no pretrial construction given
rubrics_metrics.description: Each side can present a claim interpretation and consistent evidence to a jury, avoiding evidence inconsistent with their interpretation; the jury renders a verdict based on an interpretation, and the judge can later decide claim construction post-trial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practical strategy allows the case to proceed to a jury without pretrial construction: if the judge’s post-trial construction matches the jury’s assumed interpretation, the judge will deny JMOL; if different, the judge may grant JMOL. Parties should plan evidence presentation accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markman hearings in practice are often extended oral arguments rather than full evidentiary hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: In the author's experience, 'Markman hearings are frequently extended oral arguments by advocates, and not more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect many Markman hearings to be argument-focused with limited live testimony or evidentiary development. As judges gain experience, they may rely even less on live hearings and more on written submissions and selective oral argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trend and transitional nature of routine Markman hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a broader judicial trend toward fewer live appearances and toward paper dispositions; thus 'Markman hearings as events separate from, and in advance of, trial, may in fact be a short-term phenomenon.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should be aware that the current proliferation of separate Markman hearings may decline over time; rely on jurisdictional practice and be prepared for both live hearings and paper-based adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical neutrality: hearings neither inherently beneficial nor detrimental in short term
rubrics_metrics.description: In the short term, the assumption that claim-construction hearings are necessary 'is probably not either beneficial or detrimental to the patent law, court efficiency, or specific litigants.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether to press for or oppose a separate Markman hearing should be a tactical decision based on case specifics (complexity, technical issues, local practice), not a presumptive belief that hearings always help or harm.
